lines.text: March, twenty twenty-two. Attackers drain about six hundred million dollars from the Ronin bridge.
Weeks later, the wallet that took it is on the US sanctions list. Anyone can still send it money.
Now AI agents pay in USDC. An agent sees an address. It cannot tell a vendor from a launderer.
And the checks that exist look at one wallet, once, and answer yes or no.
In one day on Arc, a hundred and fifty-four million USDC moved across nearly three thousand transfers.
Of the seven hundred and twenty-seven wallets we graded, almost half needed a limit before anyone paid them.
Money moves at machine speed. Risk checks don't. Nothing grades the counterparty, nothing keeps watching it, and no contract can check the answer.
Meet CompliR. Screen before you pay.
One call, before any payment. CompliR checks the sanctions lists, Circle's USDC blocklist, and the wallets that funded this one, two hops back.
Don't pay. This wallet is on the OFAC sanctions list, and Circle has blocked it on USDC.
Fixed rules set the score. An AI analyst sets the limits and writes the reason. It can never change the score.
Every verdict is signed, written to a registry on Arc, and added to a ledger anyone can replay. A smart contract checks it in one line.
And it keeps watching. When Circle blacklists a wallet, its grade changes within a minute.
And CompliR runs itself. An agent sets the price, under a cent a call, paid in USDC over x402. Revenue sits in Circle wallets.
It pays through a treasury that screens every payee. Asked to pay the Ronin wallet, it refused. When demand was low, it cut its own price. Twice.
Builders paste one prompt into their coding agent, and CompliR is wired in. Our sister project, Inktoll, went live on mainnet in a day.
What makes it different? Graded, not yes or no. Signed, not taken on trust. And run by an agent, in public.
CompliR. Built on Arc, with USDC and Circle. Screen before you pay.
